newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Economic misery helps fuel Serbian discontent.
newsitem.headline: Economic misery helps fuel Serbian discontent.

text.p: Plummeting living standards in Serbia have helped fuel strong popular discontent that has caused an unprecedented wave of street protests across the country, analysts said on Thursday.

A coalition of opposition parties has led more than a week of demonstrations since the authorities annulled results of a municipal poll which dealt a harsh blow to the ruling Socialists of hardline President Slobodan Milosevic.
The sharp plunge in incomes since the early 1990s had been a key factor in bringing tens of thousands of ordinary Serbs out on the streets to protest against the government, economic analysts said.

The cost of war in neighbouring Bosnia, almost four years of an international trade embargo, high inflation and obsolete industrial structures helped to cut per capita income from over $3,000 in 1990 to barely $1,500 now, economists estimate.
Average monthly salaries were less than 800 dinars ($140) in October, barely enough to pay an ordinary family's monthly utility bill.
"When you take out taxes for the army, police, education and health services, just a few dollars remain for living," an economist told Reuters on the condition of anonymity.
The latest wave of unrest is not the first time Milosevic's government had to deal with the results of what many observers see as an economic policy lying in shambles.

Thousands of workers went on strike over several months this summer, demanding payment of back wages and better working conditions in key industrial centres such as Nis, Kragujevac and the Belgrade suburbs.
A study prepared earlier this month for the Red Cross and the Red Crescent said one third of the country's population, or about three million people, still lived below the poverty line.
The study said some 30,000 people relied on soup kitchens for their day-to-day survival. Around 77 percent of those received less than 100 dinars a month for each household member.
The government insists significant improvements in Yugoslavia's economy depend on the country's speedy return to the international financial community that would enable it to draw fresh credits.
But new money alone will not do the trick, experts say.

"This is a matter of the structure of the largely state-run economy and the authorities who seem not ready to give up their firm grip on financially lucrative monopolies," one diplomat, speaking on condition of anonymity, told Reuters.
"Yugoslavia remains probably the only country to block privatisation that would shape up its economy and make it more attractive to foreign investment," he added.
